title: Kapoeta and Didinga Hills - Climate Dataset Overview and Key Numbers
content: CLIMATE DATASET FOR THE DIDINGA HILLS / KAPOETA AREA, EASTERN EQUATORIA STATE, SOUTH SUDAN. Compiled 08 August 2026 for alluvial gold mine planning. COORDINATE FOCUS: Didinga Hills range focus 4.333N 33.583E, elevation about 1961 meters; Kapoeta lowlands town reference 4.767N 33.600E, elevation about 668 meters; CRU-TS grid cell 4.25N 33.75E (0.5-degree cell) used for the long 1901-2025 record; gold-mineralisation study area (Bali, Wits MSc 2023) covers latitude 4 degrees 10 minutes to 4 degrees 45 minutes North, longitude 33 degrees 00 minutes to 34 degrees 00 minutes East, over 1000 square kilometers. KEY NUMBERS: 30-year normal 1991-2020 Didinga Hills mean annual temperature 26.3 degC, annual precipitation about 724 mm (wet season Apr-Oct about 540 mm; dry season Nov-Mar about 184 mm); 30-year normal Kapoeta lowlands mean annual temperature 28.5 degC, annual precipitation about 684 mm. Mean annual rainfall 1981-2025: Didinga Hills about 762 mm (range 412-1408); Kapoeta lowlands about 732 mm (range 339-1586); values highly variable. Driest decade 2000s (Didinga mean about 606 mm/yr); wettest period 2020s so far (Didinga mean about 951 mm/yr through 2025). National warming +1.9 degC over 1950-2020 (26.2 to 28.1 degC, World Bank CCDR 2025/26), warming rate 0.53 degC/decade over 1991-2020. Kapoeta station study (1984-2016) maximum monthly temperature increased 1.9 degC; rainfall trend decreasing. 2020 and 2024 are wettest years on record locally with severe regional flooding; 2026 running dry under strengthening El Nino. CAVEAT: local long-term station records in Kapoeta are very sparse (civil-war gap); figures blend MERRA-2 reanalysis (NASA POWER), CRU-TS v4.10 grids, national statistics (World Bank, UNDP, NAPA, FEWS NET/NOAA) and published Kapoeta-specific studies.

title: Kapoeta and Didinga Hills - Study Area Geography and Climate Setting
content: STUDY AREA GEOGRAPHY AND CLIMATE SETTING. LOCATION: Eastern Equatoria State (formerly part of Greater Kapoeta; hills lie mainly in Budi County, lowlands around Kapoeta town in Kapoeta County). Didinga Hills range coordinates 4 degrees 20 minutes North 33 degrees 35 minutes East; peak about 1961 meters above sea level (range 596-2737 meters per mountain-biodiversity database). Kapoeta town about 4.77N 33.59E, about 668 meters, about 27 km north of the hills. Gold study area (Bali 2023) 4 degrees 10 minutes to 4 degrees 45 minutes North, 33 to 34 degrees East, over 1000 square km, covering Greater Kapoeta, Didinga Hills and Dongotona Mountains. TOPOGRAPHY AND DRAINAGE: Didinga Hills are a positive-relief range of resistant basement rocks (granulites, charnockites, migmatites, gneisses, amphibolites, granitoids) with rounded dome-like hills largely devoid of vegetation. Orographic rainfall: hills receive more rain than surrounding semi-arid plains, with dense montane forest and lush grassland at altitude. Nakodok, Narus and Loyoro rivers originate on the east flank and flow east into Greater Kapoeta, discharging into swampy ground northeast of Narus; they flood in the wet season and may cease flowing in the dry season. Alluvial gold: pans and streams draining the Didinga Hills (e.g., Singatha River at the foot of the hills; Buno River system) are worked by artisanal miners; placer gold derives from quartz-vein and shear-zone mineralisation in the hills. CLIMATE SETTING (KOPPEN): Lowlands around Kapoeta are BSh (hot semi-arid / steppe); southern highlands and eastern hill margins are Aw (tropical savanna / wet-dry). Eastern Equatoria generally tropical wet-dry with a long summer wet season and a marked dry season (Nov-Mar). Mean daily temperature lowlands about 28 degC, hills about 26 degC; diurnal range large (up to about 15 degC in dry season). Rainfall: single main wet season roughly April-October (boreal summer, ITCZ-driven); pronounced dry season November-March. The southeast (Kapoeta) is the driest part of South Sudan but typically receives 450-800+ mm/yr depending on elevation. RELEVANCE TO GOLD OPERATIONS: rainfall controls stream flow in placer workings, access roads, pit flooding and water availability; heat stress controls day-labour scheduling (peak heat Mar-Apr pre-rain and hot dry months Dec-Mar in lowlands); climate change affects long-term water security, tailings/erosion management and community relations.

title: Kapoeta and Didinga Hills - Climate Trends and Decadal Analysis 1990-2025
content: TRENDS AND DECADAL ANALYSIS 1990-2025 (NASA POWER / MERRA-2). DIDINGA HILLS linear trend 1990-2025: mean temp -0.040 C per decade (essentially flat), max temp -0.007 C per decade, min temp +0.042 C per decade (slight rise in nights), precipitation +65.4 mm per decade (+8.8% per decade, wetting). Warmest year 1990-2025: 2000 (27.09 C); coldest 2020 (25.19 C); wettest 2020 (1408.3 mm); driest 2000 (412.4 mm). Decadal means Didinga Hills: 1990s precip mean 731.7 mm (min 461.7, max 951.0), Tmean 26.25 C; 2000s precip mean 606.3 mm (min 412.4, max 863.3), Tmean 26.59 C; 2010s precip mean 765.6 mm (min 621.8, max 960.2), Tmean 26.19 C; 2020s partial precip mean 950.9 mm (min 673.1, max 1408.3), Tmean 26.18 C. KAPOETA LOWLANDS linear trend 1990-2025: mean temp -0.147 C per decade, max temp -0.027, min temp -0.097, precipitation +93.8 mm per decade (+13.3% per decade, wetting). Warmest year 2000 (29.57 C); coldest 2020 (27.03 C); wettest 2020 (1586.4 mm); driest 2000 (339.3 mm). Decadal means lowlands: 1990s 683.6 mm Tmean 28.43; 2000s 530.9 mm Tmean 28.94; 2010s 736.9 mm Tmean 28.26; 2020s partial 982.3 mm Tmean 28.1. READING THE 2020s: 2020 wettest year in the whole 1981-2025 record at both sites and coldest in 1990-2025 (wet-cool anomaly, regional flood years); 2024 second wettest (Didinga 1095 mm); 2022 and 2025 near-normal; the decade 2020-2025 averages about 951 mm/yr (Didinga) vs about 606 mm/yr in the 2000s, a swing of over 55%. CAREFUL WITH TRENDS: the local 1990-2025 temperature trend is near zero in BOTH reanalysis products even though national mean temperature is rising about 0.5 C/decade, due to high interannual variability, the anomalously warm 2000s locally (2000 warmest), and station data showing the real warming signal. Do not read the flat local slope as no warming. Precipitation since 1990 shows a wetting tendency driven by the very wet 2020s, on top of large decadal swings (dry 2000s to wet 2010s/2020s), consistent with higher year-to-year variability and more intense wet years and flooding.

title: Kapoeta and Didinga Hills - Long-Term Climate Record 1901-2025 (CRU-TS v4.10)
content: LONG-TERM RECORD 1901-2025 (CRU-TS v4.10, observed station-interpolated grid cell 4.25N 33.75E covering the Didinga Hills). Source: CRU-TS v4.10 (Harris et al. 2020), University of East Anglia; UEA decade NetCDF files processed directly for 1991-2025 (monthly, complete). Independent of the NASA POWER reanalysis; the longest gridded station-observation record available for the area. PERIOD MEANS: 1901-1930 Tmean 23.25 C, Tmax 29.35, Tmin 17.21; 1991-2020 Tmean 23.99 C, Tmax 30.13, Tmin 17.89; 1991-2025 Tmean 24.08 C, Tmax 30.21, Tmin 18.00. (1931-1960 and 1961-1990 CCKP annual series unreliable, not used.) CRU CELL DECADE SERIES 1991-2025 (complete, monthly): 1990s Tmean 23.70 C Tmax 29.93 Tmin 17.53 Precip 809.4 mm; 2000s Tmean 23.99 Tmax 30.02 Tmin 18.01 Precip 870.8 mm; 2010s Tmean 24.27 Tmax 30.44 Tmin 18.15 Precip 1030.7 mm; 2020s Tmean 24.62 Tmax 30.70 Tmin 18.60 Precip 887.1 mm. CRU CELL TRENDS (per decade, linear fit 1991-2025): Tmean +0.32 C/decade, Tmax +0.28, Tmin +0.36, Precip +73 mm/decade. EXTREME YEARS 1991-2025: warmest Tmean year 2023 (25.04 C); coldest 1992 (23.58 C); hottest Tmax year 2023 (31.12 C); hottest Tmin year 2024 (19.07 C); wettest year 2020 (1395.6 mm); driest year 2016 (630.1 mm). KEY RESULT: unlike MERRA-2/POWER, the CRU grid cell DOES show sustained warming over 1991-2025, roughly +0.32 C/decade in Tmean, driven by steady warming through the 1990s-2020s. This agrees with the national warming signal and the Kapoeta station study. CRU precip 1991-2025 has large decadal swings (809 to 871 to 1031 to 887 mm), trend +73 mm/decade not statistically robust but consistent with POWER in ranking: dry 2000s, very wet 2010s/2020s, wettest 2020, driest 2016. NOTE ON CRU vs POWER: CRU cell sits on the eastern lower flank of the hills and is about 2.3 degC cooler and, in some extreme years, far wetter than the POWER point. Use CRU for the long-term trend and ranking of years; use POWER for absolute point values at the two project sites.

title: South Sudan National and Regional Climate Change Context
content: NATIONAL AND REGIONAL CLIMATE-CHANGE CONTEXT (SOUTH SUDAN). TEMPERATURE (World Bank South Sudan Country Climate and Development Report 2025/26, CRU/ERA5): average national temperature rose 1.9 degC over 70 years, from 26.2 degC (1950) to 28.1 degC (2020); warming rate accelerated from 0.37 degC/decade (1951-2020) to 0.53 degC/decade (1991-2020). South Sudan is among the world's most rapidly warming locations over the past 30 years; central and southern regions warm fastest. Mean annual national temperature varied 26.8-28.9 degC over the past 30 years; largest seasonal increases occur Dec-Mar (dry season). Heatwaves (especially March-May) increasing; February 2025 schools closed in Juba for two weeks due to heat exhaustion. Projections: about +1 degC by 2050 and about +3 degC by 2100 under SSP3-7.0 (high emissions); +0.71 to +1.35 degC by 2041-2050 depending on scenario. Tropical-night frequency rising. PRECIPITATION (national): consensus mixed for long-term rainfall; summer rainfall decreased 15-20% in parts of South Sudan (notably the northeast) since the mid-1970s (NAPA 2016, UNDP); rainfall since mid-1970s down 10-20% nationally; higher year-to-year variability; the 500 mm/yr rain belt has contracted and the arid zone is expanding southward toward the southeast (Kapoeta lies in the arid/semi-arid margin); simultaneously wet extremes and flooding increased (Sudd flood extent records 2020-2025; major floods 2021-2025). Models project a moderate rainfall increase with greater variability nationally (+0.8% to +11.8% by 2041-2050, World Bank CCDR). For the southeast (Kapoeta), NAPA places the area in the arid/semi-arid margin (mean annual rainfall just under about 450 mm in the driest border parts) with a single June-September wet season; the hills themselves get more (orographic). SEASONAL FORECAST FRAMEWORK: rainy season onset driven by the northward shift of the ITCZ / southerly to south-westerly winds (Apr-Oct); MAM and JJAS are the main forecast windows; El Nino typically brings drier conditions over much of South Sudan, La Nina near-average/above-average rainfall. ICPAC GHACOF outlooks and NOAA/FEWS NET monthly bulletins are the practical seasonal-monitoring tools. KEY NATIONAL CLIMATE-EXPOSURE FACTS: floods recorded in 1946, 1962-65, 1978-79, 1988, 1999, 2006, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2014, 2019-2025 (record Sudd floods 2020, 2021, 2022, 2024 and expected 2025); droughts increasingly frequent; about 56% of rural households surveyed (2009) cited droughts/floods as the top source of vulnerability.

title: Kapoeta and Didinga Hills - Extreme Events: Droughts, Floods and Heat
content: EXTREME EVENTS - DROUGHTS, FLOODS AND HEAT (Kapoeta / Didinga Hills). DROUGHT YEARS (NASA POWER 1981-2025): Didinga Hills driest five years: 2000 (412 mm), 2009 (448), 1993 (462), 2001, 2002; wettest five: 2020 (1408 mm), 2024 (1095), 1991 (951), 1996 (887), 2025 (863). Kapoeta lowlands driest: 2000 (339 mm), 2009 (425), 1993 (469), 2002, 2001; wettest: 2020 (1586 mm), 2024 (1067), 1991 (895), 2025, 2023. The 2000s (especially 2000, 2002, 2009) were the driest decade in the record, consistent with the 2005-2011 regional East African drought and local reports of water and pasture stress. 2020 and 2024 are the wettest years on record locally, matching record national flooding. WET-SEASON RAINFALL INTENSITY: monthly rainfall in wet years can exceed 200-300 mm/month (peak months of 2020, 2024); intense convection produces flash floods in the ephemeral streams draining the hills (Nakodok/Narus/Loyoro and the working streams of the Singatha/Buno systems). HEAT: hottest month February (lowlands max about 36-37 C, up to 40 C in extreme years); hottest season Dec-Mar and pre-rain months Mar-Apr. National context: heatwave frequency increasing, especially Mar-May (World Bank CCDR 2025/26; Juba Feb-2025 school closures). Hills are 2-3 C cooler, so heat stress is far worse in the lowlands (Kapoeta town, Singatha/Buno floodplains) than in the hill workings. FLOOD RISK NOTES: the flood-prone lowland margin of Greater Kapoeta (swamps northeast of Narus; drainage from the hills) is vulnerable in multi-year wet runs like the 2020s. No large river crosses the mine area, but ephemeral streams flood fast and cut access; bridges and fords need seasonal planning.

title: Kapoeta and Didinga Hills - Seasonal Calendar and Mining-Cycle Relevance
content: SEASONAL CALENDAR - DIDINGA HILLS / KAPOETA (typical year). JANUARY: dry, hot lowlands; near-zero rain; Tmax about 33-35 C, night low about 18 C; best overall access; water scarce; dust. FEBRUARY: driest and hottest (max about 36-37 C), minimum rain month; peak heat - schedule labour early AM; water management critical. MARCH: hot; rains start late month in hills; 2-5 rain days; pre-wet-season maintenance window. APRIL: rains build; wettest month in some records; onset typically first week of April (ICPAC); access degrading; start of pit dewatering and road hardening. MAY: rains well established; 9-15 rain days; humidity high; flooded workings risk; panning streams active. JUNE: peak rains (hills); about 10 rain days; highest working-stream flow; high water. JULY: peak rains; coolest month (min about 21 C); max stream discharge; occasional washouts. AUGUST: peak rains; coolest; high humidity; deepest dewatering need. SEPTEMBER: rains continue; onset of clear spells; wet operations continue. OCTOBER: wet season tail; second peak in lowlands (Oct wettest town record); receding waters. NOVEMBER: rains end; drying; few rain days; access improving; dust. DECEMBER: dry; hot afternoons; near-zero rain; late Dec very dry; resume normal ops; water rationing begins. RAINY SEASON SUMMARY: main wet season Apr-Oct (roughly 7 months, unimodal, boreal summer); driest 4 months Nov-Feb; normal wet-season rainfall Didinga about 540 mm of about 724 mm annual; onset forecast first week of April typical (eastern Kapoeta later in dry/failed years, e.g., 2025 delayed onset and mid-season dry spells). WATER AND ACCESS PLANNING GUIDE: Jan-Mar plan drilling, trenching, earthworks, road repairs, camp construction; water is scarce, storage planning essential. Apr-Oct placer operations run on natural stream flow but pit flooding and road loss are the main costs; budget dewatering fuel. The hills' springs and streams can support year-round water better than the lowlands; boreholes and wells in the lowlands are most stressed in Feb-Mar after a poor rainy season.

title: Kapoeta and Didinga Hills - Published Local Climate Records and Cross-Check
content: KAPOETA AND DIDINGA HILLS PUBLISHED LOCAL CLIMATE RECORDS. (1) FAO AGRIS study Changing trends in climate and livestock grazing resources in Kapoeta, South Sudan (1984-2016, Kapoeta county): maximum monthly temperature increased 1.9 degC between 1984 and 2016; rainfall trend (mean monthly) decreasing over the period (statistically non-significant at P>0.05); rainfall unreliable, droughts recurrent; reported mean annual rainfall 146.6 plus/minus 50 mm (range 54-308) which is far below all other sources and likely reflects a restricted or very dry sub-area or a data-handling issue, treat with caution; grassland cover declined about 13.6% (2000-2016); NDVI shows declining pasture density, evidence of drying and land-degradation pressures. (2) climate-data.org (Kapoeta town, 1991-2021): mean annual temperature 27.7 degC; annual rainfall about 759 mm; warmest month February (avg 30.5 C, max about 36.4 C); coolest August (avg 25.5 C); wettest month October (about 112 mm); Jul-Aug about 97 mm each; February driest (about 7 mm); max temps 35-36 C in Dec-Feb; rainfall season essentially Mar-Nov. (3) WeatherSpark (Kapoeta): typical range 21-37 degC; hottest February (about 37 C), coolest August (21 C); rainy period Feb 24 to Dec 28; peak rainfall April (2.8 inches about 71 mm); rainless period late Dec-late Feb. (4) Urbfact / other city summaries (Kapoeta, about 668 m): average temperature about 26 C; annual precipitation about 769 mm (30.3 in). (5) Didinga Hills upland (Wikipedia / regional sources): orographic enhancement - hills significantly wetter and cooler than the plains; support montane forest and perennial springs; about 1961 m summit with range up to about 2700 m; rivers Nakodok, Narus, Loyoro flood in the rains and may stop flowing in the dry season, critical for placer workings. CROSS-CHECK SUMMARY (mean annual rainfall, mm/yr): NASA POWER 1981-2025 Didinga about 762, Kapoeta lowland about 732; CRU-TS v4.10 1991-2025 cell about 850; climate-data.org 1991-2021 Kapoeta about 759; Urbfact about 769; FAO AGRIS 1984-2016 about 147 (outlier, use with caution). REALISTIC PLANNING RANGE for the mine area: 600-900 mm/yr at the lowlands, 700-1100 mm/yr in the hills, with extreme years below 450 mm (drought, e.g., 2000, 2009) and above 1400 mm (flood, e.g., 2020, 2024).

title: Kapoeta Recent Seasonal Monitoring and Outlook 2025-2026 (FEWS NET, ICPAC)
content: RECENT SEASONAL MONITORING AND OUTLOOK 2025-2026 (NOAA/FEWS NET South Sudan bulletins; ICPAC/GHACOF). 2025 SEASON: MAM 2025 (ICPAC GHACOF69 outlook) Eastern Equatoria mostly 45% above-normal rainfall, exception eastern Kapoeta East 45% below-normal; early-to-normal onset from first week of April; state-wide 45-55% probability of warmer-than-usual temperatures. January 2025 (FEWS NET): Kapoeta region (unimodal southeast) prolonged dry spells expected to hit second-season cereals; La Nina (weak) leading to near-average MAM rainfall nationally. June 2025 (FEWS NET): first phase of 2025 rains drier than average across most of South Sudan; exception Kapoeta East wetter than average early season; Eastern Equatoria dry in June in contrast to wet Mar-May. Jul-Sep 2025 (FEWS NET outlook): high likelihood of wetter-than-average core-season rains; major flood event expected in 2025 comparable to (possibly larger than) the record 2024 floods. 2026 SEASON (as of July 2026 bulletin, NOAA/FEWS NET): El Nino present and strengthening; 97% chance of persisting into early spring 2027. El Nino years bring above-average temperatures and below-average rainfall over most of South Sudan (except west). June 2026: rainfall deficits of 10-200 mm across much of the country; Eastern Equatoria among the dry areas; southern/eastern Eastern Equatoria had received above-average totals Apr-Jun (surpluses). August 2026 (NMME): 36-50% probability of below-normal rainfall over NE Eastern Equatoria (including parts of the Kapoeta area). Temperatures: June 2026 warmer than average by 3-5 degC in places (Bahr el Ghazal, Western Equatoria, Upper Nile); the eastern tip of Eastern Equatoria near average. Aug-Oct 2026: 40-70% probability of above-normal temperatures across most of the country. GEOGLAM Crop Monitor: first-season cereals degraded by early-March planting followed by dry spell to mid-May (poor germination); below-average rainfall expected nationwide through September, though the southeastern Kapoeta region remains an exception with favorable conditions. NET IMPLICATION FOR KAPOETA IN 2026: a drier, hotter season than 2025, especially in the east of the county, against a background of wet regional floods in 2024-2025. OPERATIONAL TAKEAWAY: 2026 is trending dry/hot in the Kapoeta area - prepare for water stress, heat stress and reduced stream flow in placer workings; plan drilling and earthworks early in the season. If El Nino persists into 2027, expect a second consecutive dry/hot year in the southeast - budget dewatering, water supply and heat protocols accordingly.

title: Kapoeta and Didinga Hills - Climate Implications for Gold-Mining Operations
content: IMPLICATIONS FOR GOLD-MINING OPERATIONS (Kapoeta / Didinga Hills). WATER: placer gold recovery depends on stream water. Historical and projected rainfall variability means flows in the Singatha/Buno systems and the Nakodok/Narus/Loyoro channels swing between drought shutdown (Feb-Mar, drought years) and flood damage (wet years). Recommended: seasonal water budget using the annual tables; storage tanks and ponds sized for a 450 mm/yr (2000/2009-type) year; a flood-diversion plan for the 1400 mm/yr (2020-type) year. Monitor the FEWS NET / ICPAC outlooks every March and June to adjust the season plan. HEAT AND WORKER HEALTH: peak heat Feb-Mar (lowlands max 36-37 C). With national warming (about 0.5 C/decade) and heatwave frequency rising, day-labour scheduling must shift to early morning/evening during Dec-Apr; enforce water and shade protocols; the hills sites run 2-3 C cooler than town sites. El Nino years (2026-27) add heat stress on top of the norm. ACCESS AND LOGISTICS: roads into the hills and to the Nadapal-Kapoeta highway degrade fast in Apr-Oct; budget road maintenance in Jan-Mar and late Nov. River crossings and flash-flood channels need engineering or seasonal closure; plan fuel and camp resupply before the rains. ENVIRONMENT AND COMMUNITY: climate pressure on pasture and water is already a driver of local conflict (cattle-raiding; resource competition between Toposa and Didinga) - a mine's water use and hire practices should be designed to avoid adding stress in drought years. Re-vegetation and tailings/sediment control matter most in the wet season; the hills' soil-moisture cycle supports planting from May-June onward. CLIMATE-RISK SCREENING (summary for EIA / bankability): Higher heat extremes - direction rising, confidence high (national), medium (local). Drier dry seasons and water - rising, confidence high (regional), medium (local). Rainfall variability plus wet extreme years and floods - rising, confidence high (national), high (local) since 2010s. Seasonal-onset shift - plausible, medium. Long-term rainfall change - uncertain, low-medium (models split).

title: Kapoeta Climate Dataset - Data Sources and Methods
content: DATA SOURCES AND METHODS FOR THE KAPOETA CLIMATE DATASET. PRIMARY LOCAL GRIDDED DATA: (1) NASA POWER (MERRA-2 reanalysis), AG community, monthly: Point 1 didinga_hills 4.333N 33.583E; Point 2 kapoeta_lowland 4.767N 33.600E; period 1981-01 to 2025-12 (complete 45 years; 2026 not yet released); variables T2M (mean), T2M_MIN, T2M_MAX (degC), PRECTOTCORR (mm/day converted to mm/month), RH2M (%), WS2M/WS10M (m/s), ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN (kWh/m2/day from 1984), GWETROOT (root-zone soil moisture m3/m3), PS (kPa); URL power.larc.nasa.gov. (2) CRU-TS v4.10 (University of East Anglia) observed station-interpolated grids at 0.5-degree via World Bank CCKP mirror plus UEA: grid cell 4.25N 33.75E (covers Didinga Hills); monthly tmp/pre/tmx/tmn extracted for 1991-2025 (decade files); annual series cover 1901-2025. NATIONAL / REGIONAL CONTEXT: (3) World Bank South Sudan Country Climate and Development Report (2025/26) - observed temperature 1901-2023 (26.2 C 1950 to 28.1 C 2020), warming rate 1951-2020 0.37 C, 1991-2020 0.53 C; projections to 2050 and 2100 under SSP scenarios. (4) UNDP Climate Change Country Profile / NAPA South Sudan (2016, 2017) and Technology Needs Assessment (2023) - rainfall decline 10-20% since mid-1970s; over 0.4 C/decade warming over past about 30 years in central/southern regions; flood and drought event lists. (5) NOAA/FEWS NET South Sudan Monthly Climate and Weather bulletins (Jan 2025, May 2025, Jun 2025, Jul 2026) and ICPAC GHACOF seasonal outlooks. (6) FAO AGRIS Kapoeta study (1984-2016) max-monthly temperature rise 1.9 C. (7) Station/climatology summaries: climate-data.org, WeatherSpark, Urbfact. (8) Project geology documents: Bali (2023) MSc dissertation University of the Witwatersrand; Harris et al. gossans remote-sensing paper (Geological Survey of Canada). METHODS: monthly POWER values aggregated to annual (sum for precipitation, arithmetic mean for temperature/humidity/wind/solar/soil moisture); PRECTOTCORR mm/day to mm/month (times days per month); 30-year climatological normals for WMO standard 1991-2020; linear OLS trends for 1990-2025 (POWER) and multiple windows (CRU), reported as change per decade; decadal means 1990s, 2000s, 2010s, 2020-2025 partial; CRU-TS checked against raw units, no scaling. RELIABILITY NOTES: reanalysis (MERRA-2) and station-interpolated grids (CRU) agree on the year-to-year pattern but differ in absolute value: CRU cell runs about 2.3 degC cooler and, in extreme years, differs strongly in rainfall amount. Treat local annual rainfall as plus/minus 20-40% uncertain in extreme years; direction and ranking of wet/dry years is robust. 2026 POWER data not yet published; 2026 conditions from FEWS NET/NOAA monitoring.

title: Kapoeta Gold Geology - Bali (2023) Dissertation Key Findings
content: KEY GEOLOGICAL FINDINGS FROM BALI (2023) MSc DISSERTATION, 'POTENTIAL SOURCE FOR THE ALLUVIAL GOLD DEPOSIT IN THE KAPOETA AREA', UNIVERSITY OF THE WITWATERSRAND. The rocks of Greater Kapoeta are composed of juvenile Neoproterozoic lithologies associated with the Karasuk Supergroup of the Mozambique Belt and intruded by alkaline lithologies of Neogene age. Tertiary extrusives related to the East African Rift system overlie the Karasuk Supergroup mainly to the east of the study area. The Karasuk Supergroup assemblages constitute metavolcano-sedimentary assemblages and mafic and ultramafic lithologies. Lithotypes that define the Karasuk Supergroup include gneisses, marbles, quartzites, schists, meta-basalts, meta-rhyolite, and acidic intrusions (alaskite and granites). The metasedimentary assemblages constitute rocks deposited in a shallow marine environment associated with passive margins. The metavolcanic sequences, gabbro, and the ultramafic represent part of the dismembered ophiolite suite of the Sekerr-Karamoja ophiolites described by many researchers in the border region of Karamoja of eastern Uganda and the Pokot region of western Kenya. STRUCTURE: four structural orientations are documented using satellite imagery (Landsat 8 OLI, Landsat 7 ETM and SRTM-DEM) and field validation: N-S, NW-SE, NNW-SSE, and NE-SW. The N-S and NNW-SSE trends are the potential controls on mineralisation in the area. The Karasuk Supergroup rocks in the field exhibit an N-S trending orientation with steep dips 60-70 degrees. The NW-SE lineaments are related to the Aswa and Nyangere Shear Zones, NW shear-zone patterns within the Arabian Nubian Shield, and the NE-SW structure to the east of Didinga Hills resembles the Aswa shear zone. MINERALISATION STYLE: gold mineralisation of Kapoeta is orogenic in nature with a strong element of epigenetic characteristics, although a syngenetic origin cannot be ruled out. The host lithologies may vary from quartz veins to schists, amphibolites, quartzo-feldspathic gneisses, ultramafics, and the marbles, all related to the N-S, NNW-SSE and NW-SE trending shear zones that limit the greenstone belt. PATHFINDERS: the distribution of Cu, Co, Cr, Ni and Zn and their high concentration, plus pyrite enrichment, suggest these are the potential pathfinders for gold mineralisation. GEOCHEMISTRY: most lithologies belong to an island arc, continental arc and mid-oceanic ridge sequences dominated by sub-alkaline tholeiite series; whole-rock data plotted on TAS diagrams shows dominantly tholeiitic with minor calc-alkaline units; trace elements normalized to primitive mantle show low concentrations of Zr, Hf, Nb and Ta; REE show enrichment of LREE relative to HREE with a negative Eu anomaly; tectonic discrimination diagrams indicate a marine environment related to a spreading centre, oceanic island, oceanic ridge, and oceanic floor. RECOMMENDATIONS: detailed geological mapping of the entire area underlain by Karasuk Supergroup lithologies is needed; more geochemical studies of the metavolcano-sedimentary assemblages and associated intrusions; security issues related to cattle rustling hinder free movement of researchers.

title: Kapoeta Gold Occurrences - Documented Mineralisation Sites and Grades
content: DOCUMENTED GOLD OCCURRENCES, SITES AND GRADES IN THE KAPOETA AREA (from Bali 2023 dissertation and legacy survey reports). PREVIOUS STUDIES found 12 localities of gold occurrences associated with different lithologies in the Kapoeta area. The most important gold deposit was the Kawokono, about 45 km east of Kapoeta town and 3 km south of the Lobur police post. Gold occurs in both eluvial and alluvial concentrations. The primary source is hosted in graphitic gneisses invaded by an NW-SE trending alaskite body (Adde 2002). A follow-up investigation in a small portion yielded an average of 6.5 g Au per cubic meter. Adde (1984) investigated the minerals, structures and rock types associated with Kapoeta gold, while Kwaku (1986) outlined that the acid/basic rocks are chemically associated with the Kapoeta. The Belgian Geological Survey mineral exploration mission conducted an exploration campaign between 1979-1985 with extensive geochemical sampling and analysis of stream sediments; several alluvial and eluvial gold occurrences were found; an effort to continue the project was frustrated by the civil war of 1983 to 2005. The unpublished reports of the Belgian Mineral Exploration Project (1983, 1985) found gold hosted in eluvium and alluvium with concentrations of 2.5 g/m3 and 1 to 2 g/m3 associated with talc schists. In Nyangea, about 25 km ENE of Kapoeta town, the eluvial gold deposit occurs in quartz veins hosted in talc and chlorite schist. Adde (1984) suggested the occurrence of tremolite-actinolite may be used as a pathfinder for gold; tremolite-actinolite minerals suggest provenance from schists and greenstone host rocks. Heavy metals (probably magnetite and other ferromagnesian minerals) after panning suggest mineralisation is lithologically linked to mafic minerals originating from basic and ultrabasic rocks south of the Buno stream. The Kawokono gold deposit is hosted in marbles and NW-SE trending graphitic gneiss intruded by alaskite (Belgian Mineral Exploration Project 1985). Deposits at the anticline can be considered as dual mineralisation involving intrusion of granitic composition lithologies (alaskite) into marble, including marble and quartzo-feldspathic gneiss. PRODUCTION: the Belgian Geological Survey Mineral Exploration (1980) estimates artisanal miners' gold produced from this region from placer deposits between 1979 to 1983 amounts to approximately 100-200 kg per annum. Placer gold divides into three groups: gold panned in stream beds suggesting transport from upstream; gold panned from overlying sediments (possibly eluvial) deposited simultaneously with overburden over the Karasuk Supergroup; and gold recovered from ancient streams buried under overburden, with an example at Kaitap where artisanal miners dig.

title: Detecting and Mapping Gossans - Remote Sensing Methods (Harris et al., GSC)
content: REMOTE SENSING METHODS FOR DETECTING AND MAPPING GOSSANS (Harris, Williamson, Percival, Behnia, Macleod, Geological Survey of Canada). Gossans are surficial deposits that form in host rocks by the oxidation of sulphides by acidic and oxidizing fluids. In a classic gossan profile, primary sulphides are replaced by iron-bearing pseudomorphs such as ferrihydrite, goethite and jarosite. Gossans are important vectors to buried ore deposits, and many mineral deposits have been found by mapping gossans. IMAGE PROCESSING TECHNIQUES: (1) Natural colour composites (wavelength matched to RGB) produce a colour image as seen by the human eye. (2) Band ratios: the Red/Blue ratio (Landsat 7 bands 3/1) highlights gossans by leveraging high reflection of red energy (why gossans appear in shades of red, orange and yellow) and strong absorption of blue energy; in the High Lake case this revealed 10 additional smaller gossans. (3) Principal Component Analysis (PCA; Crosta and Moore 1989): apply PCA transform and select the component image with negative loading (eigenvector) for the blue band and a high positive weighting for the red band. (4) Supervised classification: use representative reflectance spectra of known gossans (from spectral libraries of iron oxide minerals or from the imagery itself) and classify similar signatures. CAUTION: other targets with similar spectral responses to gossans can be misidentified - red to yellow geological units (shale, sandstone), surficial deposits (eolian, glaciofluvial, littoral sediments) and vegetation (bogs). These false targets must be screened out using more detailed spectral and pattern analysis. HYPERSPECTRAL MAPPING: with sufficient spectral resolution, individual iron oxides can be uniquely identified by their spectral characteristics in the VNIR portion of the electromagnetic spectrum. Jarosite, hematite and goethite can be uniquely identified by spectral reflectance characteristics with absorptions and reflection peaks at specific wavelengths, caused by electronic transitions and charge transfer processes associated with transition elements, particularly Fe. With hyperspectral data you can move from detecting gossans to identifying the predominant minerals in the oxide cap (e.g., matching extracted spectra to USGS spectral library, often goethite). APPLICATION TO KAPOETA: in the Kapoeta area, Landsat-8 OLI and SRTM-DEM were successfully employed to map lithological units, highlight hydrothermal alteration, and outline structural trends. Band ratio B4/B2 highlights ferric oxides (ilmenites, hematite) from intense surface oxidation, widespread in artisanal mining areas restricted to weathered or altered metasediments. Band ratio B6/B7 refers to clay minerals, of which kaolinites are the most abundant. Lighter-toned pixels coincide with hydrothermal alteration zones characterized by silicification, quartz veins, sericite, and pyrite (Hunting Geology and Geophysics Ltd 1980). Areas east and southeast of Kapoeta are known artisanal gold mining sites appearing as altered, iron-oxide-rich zones.

title: Kapoeta Climate Dataset - Data Dictionary and File Listing
content: DATA DICTIONARY AND FILES FOR THE KAPOETA CLIMATE DATASET. Plain-text documents (docs folder): 00 README and INDEX; 01 STUDY AREA geography and climate setting; 02 DATA SOURCES AND METHODS; 03 ANNUAL CLIMATE TABLE 1981-2025 DIDINGA HILLS (NASA POWER/MERRA-2); 04 ANNUAL CLIMATE TABLE 1981-2025 KAPOETA LOWLANDS; 05 MONTHLY CLIMATOLOGY 1991-2020 (30-YEAR WMO NORMAL); 06 TRENDS AND DECADAL ANALYSIS 1991-2025; 07 LONG-TERM RECORD 1901-2025 (CRU-TS v4.10 OBSERVED GRIDDED DATA); 08 NATIONAL CLIMATE-CHANGE CONTEXT (WORLD BANK / UNDP / NAPA); 09 KAPOETA AND DIDINGA HILLS PUBLISHED LOCAL RECORDS; 10 EXTREME EVENTS DROUGHTS, FLOODS AND HEAT; 11 SEASONAL CALENDAR; 12 RECENT SEASONAL MONITORING AND OUTLOOK 2025-2026 (NOAA/FEWS NET, ICPAC); 13 IMPLICATIONS FOR GOLD-MINING OPERATIONS; 14 REFERENCES; 15 DATA DICTIONARY AND FILES. DATA FILES (data folder): cckp_cru_pr_annual_1901_2025.nc, cckp_cru_pr_monthly_heatplot_1901_2025.nc, cckp_cru_tas_annual_1901_2025.nc, cckp_cru_tas_monthly_heatplot_1901_2025.nc, cckp_cru_tasmax_annual_1901_2025.nc, cckp_cru_tasmin_annual_1901_2025.nc (NetCDF CRU grids); cckp_ssd_cru_pr_annual_1901_2022.json, cckp_ssd_cru_tas_annual_1901_2022.json, cckp_ssd_era5_pr_annual_1950_2023.json, cckp_ssd_era5_tas_annual_1950_2023.json (World Bank CCKP summaries); climate_summary_computed.json; cru_analysis_didinga_1901_2025.json; cru_didinga_cell_annual_1901_2025.json; cru_didinga_monthly_1991_2025.json; cru_ts4.10 decade NetCDF files (1991-2000, 2001-2010, 2011-2020, 2021-2025) for pre/tmn/tmp/tmx; didinga_hills_annual_1981_2025.csv and didinga_hills_monthly_1981_2025.csv (NASA POWER point data); kapoeta_lowland_annual_1981_2025.csv and kapoeta_lowland_monthly_1981_2025.csv; power_didinga_east_lowland_monthly_1981_2025.json, power_didinga_hills_monthly_1981_2025.json, power_didinga_west_lowland_monthly_1981_2025.json, power_kapoeta_lowland_monthly_1981_2025.json; extended_analysis_sites.json. CSV COLUMNS: annual files have year, tmean, tmax, tmin, precip_mm, rh2m, ws2m, sw_insol, soilmoist. Monthly files have year, month, tmean, tmin, tmax, precip_mm, precip_mmday, rh2m, ws2m, ws10m, sw_insol, soilmoist, ps. SUMMARY DOCUMENTS (dataset_summaries folder): didinga_east_lowland.md, didinga_hills.md, didinga_west_lowland.md, kapoeta_lowland.md. CHART IMAGES (charts folder): annual mean temperature trend, annual precipitation trend, monthly climatology, decadal precipitation, temperature anomaly, precipitation extremes. IMAGES (images folder): project location map, South Sudan relative location map, FEWS NET South Sudan Current bulletin PDF and page screenshots.
